name: Adam Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a cell of six CNC lathes and mills making pump housings and impellers, and I check tool wear before a batch drifts out of tolerance. I have a two-year technical diploma and fourteen years at Brennan Pumps, and my skill is among the strongest on the floor. The wage is about normal for an operator, though I supervise five people.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and how do you use new technology?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Leila is a nurse, and our school-age children Noah and Sara live with us under a mortgage. We have about four months saved and some other machining shops nearby. I use a phone AI tool now and then for alarm codes, then check the manual before changing a setting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the machining team that a useful alarm-code hint is worth keeping, but it does not measure an impeller for us. I would want the saved office time reflected in the next pay meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead six machines and can hear tool chatter early, so a quiet AI outcome leaves our plant much as it is. Leila’s nursing shifts and my ordinary lead wage cover the mortgage, and four months saved gives us breathing space.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking first-off parts and use my existing chat app for alarm codes, then verify them in the manual. From each full paid month we would put a fresh amount against mortgage principal, and I would take our downtime figures to the union pay meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel calm about the job. We have enough set aside to handle a bad car month without borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How accurate is the app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gets a likely cause about twice in three tries. I still read the controller alarm and ask Ruth in inspection before changing a setting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach the rest of the team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already tell them which alarm hints are wrong. That is ordinary shift handover, not a new course for me.

say: I would keep **alarm hints** only when the manual backs them.
I would bring **saved downtime** into pay talks.
think: My **lead skills** still matter at the machines.
Leila’s **nursing shifts** and four months saved make ordinary shocks manageable.
do: Check **first impellers** and controller alarms on six machines.
Keep using the **existing chat app** after manual checks.
Pay extra **mortgage principal** from fresh full-month wages.
feel: **Calm** about work and a four-month reserve.
S0.quote: We have enough set aside to handle a bad car month without borrowing.
fieldNote: Adam’s **technical diploma** and fault-finding skill anchor his lead role.
His app use is an **existing habit**, while extra mortgage payments use current paid wages.

Pay extra mortgage principal from fresh full-month wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our union meeting that ordering software may change office jobs first, while robot loaders spread into machining more slowly. If the company gains hours, the crew should see a paid transfer route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the team could drop from five to three if loaders work, though they may still need me to set the cells. I would feel for the two people moved, and I would ask whether my own hours or pay are protected in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my machining shift and bring current staffing figures to the union. If Brennan offers a funded supplier course with paid time and an actual guarded practice place after one robot cell proves it can cut a sound part, I would enrol and learn its new controls; I would put fresh spare wages into savings while the rota stays full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy because my own work looks steady but the team may change. I owe them more than a cheerful story about a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you to train?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A clean measured part from the first cell and a qualified setter beside me at a stopped machine. I would not take a video in place of an offered paid practice shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if two colleagues are displaced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the branch for posted local vacancies and make introductions only with their agreement. A friendly phone call is not a promised job.

say: I would demand a **paid transfer route** before loaders cut the team.
I would keep **office AI** separate from later robot work.
think: The crew may shrink from **five to three**.
My own **lead hours** look likely to continue, though I want written terms.
do: Keep **machining shifts** and bring staffing figures to the union.
Enrol in **funded paid supplier training** only after an offered safe place and proven cell.
feel: **Uneasy** for colleagues while his own pay looks secure.
S1.quote: I owe them more than a cheerful story about a machine.
fieldNote: He waits for a **measured good part** before learning new robot controls.
Training requires an **offered paid guarded place**; union action seeks actual vacancies for displaced colleagues.

steps.text: Bring current staffing figures to union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union that thinking AGI in 2028 could write our machining programs, while capable hands-on robots reach the lathe cells around 2031. The two dates matter to a team that still loads and measures metal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the programming part of my paid work to shrink first and most cell hours to go when robots can set and check parts. Four months saved and Leila’s nursing wage will not cover our mortgage and both children for a long loss; I would lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel the second-car replacement and school trip and ask for written staffing dates. If my shifts end, I would apply only for posted reachable machining or maintenance work with net pay after travel covering our bills; if no adequate job appears, I would ask the lender about temporary terms and join the union’s wage-support campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by the likely loss of a big part of my wage. I can ask for help, but I cannot make the next firm need a machinist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Leila work more nursing shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She would have to check the ward rota and who picks up Sara. I would not put unoffered shifts into our mortgage budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would manual lathe work survive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for a while, but I would apply only if an actual local shop posts a paid place and the take-home amount is enough. The old skill by itself is not an offer.

say: I would separate **2028 programming AGI** from 2031 hands-on robots.
I would seek **written staffing dates** before the cell shrinks.
think: I expect **programming pay** to fall before most physical machine hours.
Four **months saved** and one nursing wage cannot bridge a long gap.
do: Cancel **car and trip** and request staffing dates.
Apply after **lost shifts** only for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work.
Ask **lender and union** for temporary help if no adequate job appears.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless household sums.
S2.quote: I can ask for help, but I cannot make the next firm need a machinist.
fieldNote: His **desk-side programming** changes before 2031 robots threaten physical cell work.
Nursing overtime, local vacancies and mortgage relief remain **conditional offers**, never counted as certain income.

steps.text: Cancel car replacement and school trip and request staffing dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the branch that thinking AGI in 2031 and capable machine robots around 2034 give time to bargain for training before the cuts. I would want actual places with paid hours on the noticeboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At forty-eight I would still have the mortgage and school costs. Electrical installation might earn a few more years, but I would not leave a steady cell for a course unless the new work had customers and usable pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my machining wage and put new full-month surplus against mortgage principal. If the college offers me a funded electrical-installation seat outside paid shifts, Leila’s rota covers the children, a qualified electrician offers safe isolated practice, and a posted reachable role has bill-covering net pay, I would enrol; after qualifying, I would apply for that role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious but able to check a real route over five years. The first cable I touch should be dead, and the first job should have a wage written on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your brother-in-law Sami hire you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami has paid work on some weeks, but I would need a written offer and net pay after materials and travel before I left Brennan. A family conversation is not a full order book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no funded seat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my paid machining shifts and search posted local operator work if the cell starts losing hours. I would not spend the mortgage reserve on tuition.

I would separate **2031 thinking work** from later physical loss.
think: The **mortgage and school costs** remain at forty-eight.
Electrical work needs **adequate net pay**, not a family promise.
do: Keep **machining shifts** and pay extra mortgage principal from new wages.
Enrol in **funded electrical training** only outside paid shifts, with an offered place, childcare, supervised isolated practice and adequate posted role.
Apply after **qualification** for reachable electrical work; leave only for a written offer covering bills after materials and travel.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to check the course and real work.
S3.quote: The first cable I touch should be dead, and the first job should have a wage written on it.
fieldNote: He seeks **electrical practice** only through funded training and qualified safe isolation.
The later **application** needs a posted reachable job and net pay after travel; Sami’s possible work is not guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AGI in 2036 and capable machining robots around 2039 give us a decade to demand good training and fair transfers. A longer clock should mean written places, not another poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be fifty-three when the thinking systems arrive and fifty-six when robots may run the cells. Noah and Sara will be adults, but our mortgage balance, Leila’s rota and my health are not things I can guarantee today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the cell running and pay a fresh extra amount toward the mortgage from full wages. If I am offered a funded electrical course on paid shift time with safe supervised practice and a posted reachable bill-covering net-pay job, I would enrol and apply after qualifying; in the first year after 2036, if still employed, I would compare actual hours with local postings and apply after sustained cuts only for adequate safe work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about the far robots while our present pay remains sound. Ten years lets me test wiring work before I put the house on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check pension and mortgage figures closer to the time. If our bills still require my wage, I would keep working in a safe paid role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell younger operators?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show them the paid course list and the actual vacancy board. A training promise without a job at the other end is not enough for a family.

I would keep **2036 thinking AI** separate from later cell work.
think: Our **mortgage and nursing rota** may look different years ahead.
The long runway lets me **test electrical work** without assuming success.
do: Keep **2026 cell shifts** and pay extra mortgage from fresh wages.
Enrol in **funded safe electrical training** only with workable timing and adequate posted job.
Apply after **post-2036 cuts** only for posted reachable safe bill-covering work.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant robots while current wages remain sound.
S4.quote: Ten years lets me test wiring work before I put the house on it.
fieldNote: His **2026 machining work** is current, while later rota checks require continued employment.
Course entry and later applications retain **real conditions**: offered funding, paid time, safe practice, posted reachable work and bill-covering net wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because programming may shrink before capable robots reach the physical cells around 2031. Written staffing dates, funded safe training and posted reachable bill-covering work would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whose knowledge ends up in the robot’s instructions. I can hear a lathe chatter before a tool breaks, and I want the apprentices to learn that sound.

headlineQuote: I can hear a lathe chatter before a tool breaks, and I want the apprentices to learn that sound.
portrait: **Adam**, 43, leads a pump-parts machining cell with a two-year technical diploma and unusually strong fault-finding skill.
His **nurse partner**, two school-age children, mortgage, ordinary pay and four-month reserve give a short but useful bridge.
He uses **AI occasionally** for alarm codes and learns robot controls only after a proven cell and offered paid guarded training.
Fast AGI threatens **programming pay first**; longer warning supports conditional electrical training and extra mortgage payments.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut programming hours before capable robots threaten most machining shifts around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, funded safe instruction and posted reachable work at bill-covering net pay would help.
